message.content:
The number of distinct positions that can arise in a game of chess is astronomically large.  In 1950 Claude Shannon famously estimated that the game has a “Shannon number” of about  

\[
N_{\text{Shannon}}\;\approx\;10^{43}
\]

legal positions.  Subsequent research and computer enumeration have refined this estimate:

| Category | Rough count |
|----------|-------------|
| **All legal positions** (including all possible piece placements, castling rights, en‑passant squares, and side to move) | ≈ 10^46 |
| **All positions (legal + illegal)** | ≈ 10^47 |
| **Positions reachable from the starting position** (i.e., those that can actually occur in a real game) | ≈ 10^43 – 10^44 |

So, while the exact number is still a subject of research, the consensus is that there are on the order of **10^43 to 10^46** distinct arrangements that can appear in a chess game.
